fatal_errors: The proposed Hf-to-Al substitution does not reconstruct the target intervention of adding 4.2 at.% Cr by vacuum arc melting.
It assumes retention of a single-phase BCC solid solution and therefore misses the target reticulated Cr2(Ti,Zr,Hf,Ta) Laves phase and its crack-arrest/plasticity-compensation role.
The loading mode is left as tensile or compressive, making the strength thresholds non-comparable because the reported baseline and target results are compression-specific.
The composition definition is inconsistent: x = 0.10-0.20 as a fraction of the Hf site is not equivalent to replacing Hf with 10-20 at.% Al in the whole alloy.
The rejection rule incorrectly rejects the hypothesis if any tested composition misses the targets, even though the hypothesis only requires that an optimal controlled substitution level succeed.
explanation: The hypothesis directly addresses the stated engineering trade-off by attempting to lower density while retaining room- and high-temperature strength, and Al substitution is a scientifically plausible alternative. E2 supports density reduction and improved specific strength from Al in other RHEAs, but it does not establish retention of absolute yield strength at 1000 °C in HfMoTaTiZr. E1 emphasizes refractory, high-melting-point elements for elevated-temperature strength and thus does not substantiate the proposed Al-based high-temperature mechanism. Relative to the hidden target, the intervention, secondary-phase morphology, ductility mechanism, and quantitative outcomes are absent: the target uses Cr addition to create about 3.8-4 vol.% reticulated Laves phase, producing approximately 13.5% higher yield strength and 20.6% higher fracture strain under room-temperature compression. The proposed experiment has useful quantitative density and strength thresholds, but ambiguous loading, strain rate, processing, and composition definitions weaken discriminability.
